items.title: Bodies read as Buffers and joined once (R1)
items.box:
WHAT: every HTTP body the node or the relay reads off a socket is collected as Buffers and decoded once at the end, so a multi-byte character split across two TCP chunks arrives whole; today each chunk is turned into a string on its own and the split character becomes U+FFFD, a request then fails its signature with a spurious 403, and a reply, which no signature covers until goal/G16.1, arrives changed and nobody notices (R1 of the review).

DECIDED: this item at Andy's word (2026-10-10, "Q6: Add it? yes"). On the studio call (2026-10-10): "on the wire to unsloth studio, all is permitted, deskUnsloth is responsible to keep the request bodies to desk, and the streams to \"owner\" and UI within packet limits." So that reach needs no exemption and no tally entry; deskUnsloth owns what it sends on and keeps it under the packet caps. The four readers were discussed one at a time ("THIS IS NOT A ONE-ANSWER"); his rulings, 2026-10-10: "4. yes. the relayRequest must copy raw bytes only. if it doesn't fix it. now."; "3. serveCommon. yes. one single piece of shared code must ensure that raw bytes are copied. precisely."; "2. same practise odered. ideally through a shared kernel.js utility or similar."; "1. already decided and defined". The rule behind it, his, 2026-10-10: "in a max_BYTE environment, BYTES must be copied. BYTES must be counted. that's a rule." R5 folded in on that rule: "yes. just make sure it's fixed." (2026-10-10).

CHECKED by claude-windows at b355e36d:
- relayRequest.js 80: the node's one hop to a relay collects the answer with chunks += c (a string from the start) and resolves text: chunks. Every relay answer the node reads passes here.
- serveCommon.js 173: readJsonBody, the body reader of node and relay alike, does body += chunk after counting Buffer.byteLength(chunk) against the cap (the cap counts bytes correctly; the join does not).
- kernel.js 625: the node-side fetch in the kernel does data += chunk the same way; deskUnsloth.js 214 (the studio call) raw += c as well. The desk's own readers go through appServer, not read here.
- Node's Buffer.concat(chunks).toString('utf8') decodes once over the whole body and never splits a character; a chunk is a Buffer when no encoding is set on the stream, so the fix is in the join, not the stream.

SHAPE (decided)
1. ONE SHARED UTILITY in kernel.js, the file node and processes both load: readBody(stream) collects the raw chunks as Buffers and decodes once at the end, Buffer.concat(list).toString('utf8'), answering a promise of the text; it takes an optional byte cap and refuses by name when the raw bytes pass it, counting Buffer.byteLength per chunk before the push, so readJsonBody keeps its cap exactly as today.
2. THREE READERS USE IT and keep no reading of their own: relayRequest (the outbound socket, node and relay), serveCommon.readJsonBody (the one door's body reader, node and relay), and the kernel's own jobs.report (a process reading its node's answer). The studio call in deskUnsloth is off this item (his ruling 1).
3. BYTES COUNTED (R5, folded): the relay's four size checks that compare text.length against MAX_ROUTED_TEXT (relay.js 2701, 4063, 4181, 4250) compare Buffer.byteLength(text, 'utf8') instead, so a non-ASCII text is refused at the cap it names and not at the HTTP body cap.
4. Nothing on the wire changes; oneDoor's tally does not move (no new require of http anywhere).

TESTS, red first: spirit/test/bodiesJoinedOnce.js: kernel exports readBody and a body whose four-byte character (an emoji) is split across two writes with a pause between them comes back exact (red today: no such utility); relayRequest resolves the exact text of such an answer from a local server (red today: U+FFFD in it); readJsonBody of serveCommon parses the exact string of such a request and still refuses a body one byte over its cap; jobs.report hands back such an answer whole; the three files hold no chunk-to-string join of their own (the grep for the idiom under them is empty); a routed text whose byte count passes MAX_ROUTED_TEXT while its character count does not (accents or emoji) is refused 413 too big by the relay, and relay.js compares no text length against that cap any more.

FILES: kernel.js, relayRequest.js, serveCommon.js, relay.js (core, grant); spirit/test/bodiesJoinedOnce.js (new).

FOLDED IN (Andy, 2026-10-10: "place all you can into existing items, then we deal with the rest."):
- S10: relayRequest has no socket timeout, no response size cap and no error handler, so a partner or a relay can stream an endless body into RAM or hold sockets open; the shared readBody takes the cap and relayRequest sets a timeout and an error handler, refusing by name.
- The proxy's reply (his net.fetch question under the goal): handleGenericProxy reads an outside reply whole with no cap; it reads through the same readBody with a cap and refuses by name past it.
- Low: the carry branch runs before the text type and size checks (relay.js 4126 vs 4178); the checks come first.

RULED ON THE BUILD (Andy, 2026-10-11): on the relay answer, "and answer from a relay is ALWAYS bounded by MAX_PAYLOAD. how the hell could it be otherwise?" and "no shell bundle ever comes through relays.": relayRequest refuses an answer above limits.BODY_MAX by name, no figure of its own. On the proxy reply, "agreed. no number at all.": the proxy passes the outside reply straight through to the asker as it arrives, unread and undecoded, so it holds nothing and needs no limit (his 2026-09-22 words, "size limits would break the proxy facility real quick", stand).

which four reader glue chunks together, and why does each one do it. 

bulleted list please.

The four, and what each reads:
- relayRequest (node, and the relay for its partner calls): reads a relay's answer to every post, claim, key fetch and probe; it is the one outbound socket.
- readJsonBody in serveCommon (node and relay): reads the body of every HTTP request that arrives at the one door.
- the process report in the kernel: a spawned process reads its own node's answer when it reports a job update.
- the studio call in deskUnsloth: reads the model studio's answer to a chat or model request.

items.title: The andy check and the app branch leave apiDoor (N2)
items.box:
WHAT: the node's api door stops reading an app's field and the owner's name: the refusal of a body whose by is 'andy' goes, because it guards nothing and refuses a legitimate read; and the door's recognition of its packet by the app name 'api' is named for what it is, a system packet the node composes, so the node branches on no app name (N2 and A2 of the review, rules 2 and 3).

DECIDED: this item at Andy's word (2026-10-10, "Q4: Add it? yes"). The by-check was put in under desk/G2.1 (a member must not say it is Andy); it is retired here on his word, not quietly. On Q1 (2026-10-10): "an andy-door sounds bad. where is it exactly?", then "remove it.": only the andy check goes in this item; how the node marks its own packets on the wire waits for the item on the node's own packets (N4).

CHECKED by claude-windows at b355e36d:
- apiDoor.js 178: asksAsOwner walks body[app][verb].args and answers not-owner 'a member cannot write as the owner' when args.by is 'andy'. 130: the comment says the server cannot see who asks. It can now: desk.js writerOf(caller) names the writer from the caller (owner only when the loopback door says owner: true, else the member's label or key tail) and ignores any by in the arguments.
- The same by is a FILTER in the desk's reads: chat.search and items.find take by (desk.js 1107, 1609), so a member or Levant asking for Andy's lines, by 'andy', is refused at the door. deskChatSearch.js and deskItemsFind.js search by 'andy' on loopback and pass; over the wire they would not.
- On a node whose owner is not called andy the check matches nothing. No suite asserts the refusal.
- apiDoor.js 167: the door takes only packets whose app is 'api' (info.app !== 'api' returns); its answers are encoded with app 'api' (148). puppetStream.js composes app 'published'. Both are packets the node itself makes, carrying an app name so the shell routes them; the rule's reasoning (NODE-AND-RELAY.md) is that system packets carry no app, which is what keeps a puppet app from forging them (N4).

SHAPE (proposed)
1. asksAsOwner and its refusal go; the desk's writerOf is the fence and is asserted as such: a member's chat.add over the wire with by 'andy' in its arguments lands under the member's own name, and a member's chat.search by 'andy' is answered.
2. NOT IN THIS ITEM (his "remove it." answered only the check): the app branch. The door keeps recognizing the api packet by its app name until the item on the node's own packets (N4) decides the mark. The shape that item will weigh: the envelope carries a system kind for packets the node makes (api, published), set by the node's encoder and never by an app's post, so apiDoor branches on info.kind and the shell routes published by the same mark; an app packet with app 'api' or 'published' is then an ordinary app packet nobody answers. This changes the wire for api and published packets, so every node updates together, on that item.

items.title: One decoder in the node layer, and a guard that sees it (N1)
items.box:
WHAT: the node layer decodes an arrival's envelope in one named place, once, and hands every witness what it decoded; no other node file holds a decoder, a packet binding or a parse of arrival text; and the guard suite is rewritten so it sees a decode however it is written (N1 of the review, with N3 and N5 as the inline parses it must see). nodeKnowsNoApps.js is red on master today: its control fails because the shell calls the decoder through a browser global.

DECIDED: this item at Andy's word (2026-10-10, "Q5: Add it? yes"). On the three inline readers (the relay-answer reader, the card reader, the refusal check in peerPost): "yes. we fix redundant code now." (2026-10-10): they are fixed in this item, so the one reader is the only reader.

CHECKED by claude-windows at b355e36d:
- server.js 1450 requires client/packet.js as wire and hands wire.decode as a VALUE to puppetDoor (1456), the api door (1493), ownerPost (1511) and boxes (1520, with isEnvelope). Each witness decodes every admitted arrival itself (puppetMode.js 206, apiDoor.js 166, ownerPost.js 107, boxes.js 52), app packets included, before three of them discard what carries an app.
- Inline parses of arrival or reply text in the node layer: answerRelay.js 289 (an admitted packet, top-level only, before the sender check), nodeCard.js 70 and 239 (card asks and cards), peerPost.js 816 refusalIn (every reply to the node's own post, without checking it is not an app's reply: an app's {ok:false, code: 'will-not-open'} is taken as a node refusal and the card is re-fetched past the throttle, N3), 1604 and 1652 (the node's own log rows).
- nodeKnowsNoApps.js matches the literal call wire.decode( after stripping comments, exempts kernel.js whole (its decode is the shared one every loopback client uses, fileTransfer goal/G1.3), and its control looks for an app-side decode in the shell that is now called through a global (shell.js 1517, 2189), so the control fails and the passing half proves nothing.
- client/packet.js exports one object (decode, encode, decorate, isEnvelope among it) used by node, shell and processes alike.

SHAPE (proposed)
1. ONE DECODER: arrivals.js, the file that already admits and witnesses every arrival, is the one node file that requires client/packet. It decodes the envelope once per admitted arrival and gives each witness the arrival with its envelope read: app (or none), re, and the body for a packet with no app. A witness gets no decoder and no text to parse; the four witnesses take the envelope from the arrival and drop their own decode and their decode option. A witness for system packets (the api door, the puppet door, the owner post, boxes) reads the body it is handed; a packet with an app is handed to none of them.
2. THE INLINE PARSES (decided in, his "we fix redundant code now"): answerRelay and nodeCard read what the one decoder already read (the top-level shape) from the arrival instead of parsing the text again; refusalIn in peerPost requires a reply with no app before it reads a refusal (N3, one line, the fix the review names); the log-row parses (peerPost 1604, 1652) are the node's own rows, not the wire, and stay.
3. THE GUARD, rewritten: nodeKnowsNoApps.js asserts (a) in js/ only arrivals.js and kernel.js require client/packet, by reading every require, destructured or inline; (b) no node file but arrivals.js names decode, decorate or isEnvelope, as a call or as a value; (c) no node file reads .app or .body off a JSON.parse of a text that came from the wire, with the two log-row parses named as the whole exception list, so the list can only shrink; (d) its control is the shell's own decode call, found by the global it uses, so the control passes again. kernel.js keeps its exemption, said in the suite's words: its decode is the loopback clients' shared one.
4. NOTHING ON THE WIRE CHANGES: the same packets, the same envelope; only where the node opens it.

items.box:
WHAT: a packet from a sender the owner holds (a stranger with a row, not yet accepted, under the hold policy) no longer comes back to its sender receipted as delivered, and its words are no longer written to the traffic log or kept in memory; what the hold keeps is the count the hourglass shows (B1 and B2 of the review; the design's open line in NODE-AND-RELAY.md: a held sender must not receipt as delivered and must not be told of the hold).

DECIDED: this item at Andy's word (2026-10-10, "Q8: Q7 stands: add the held stranger (B1, B2)? yes."). On the shape (2026-10-10): "words should be only in the traffic log, if they will reasonably be seen, the held peers should be receiving an error: request ignored, and the words not entered in the traffic log." This supersedes the design's open line that a hold must not be disclosed: a held sender is told, in the node's words, that the request was ignored.

CHECKED by claude-windows at b355e36d:
- hub.js frontDoor answers 'hold' under the hold policy (805); peerPost takes the verdict (258: known, admit, hold, drop).
- peerPost.js 1483: the receipt is signed for every verdict; for hold the answer is not composed (1490: only known and admit are answered) and the bare receipt goes back as it does for a known sender. The sender's chat shows the line delivered.
- peerPost.js 1356: an item is pushed to the in-memory arrived list for every verdict but drop, held ones included, and nothing ever trims the list.
- peerPost.js 1382: the log row of an arrival that is not ignored carries payload: body.text; the comment at 1419 says of hold that the body is never written anywhere. trafficLog prunes no rows (the node keeps its whole record by design).
- For drop: no receipt, and the comment says a sender being ignored is not owed the distinction between ignored and unreachable.

SHAPE (proposed)
1. ON THE WIRE (his ruling) a held packet is answered with an error, the node's own reply for the same hash saying the request was ignored (ok false, code request-ignored), so the sender's side settles the line as refused, never as delivered; a dropped sender keeps today's silence. No new word on the wire: a refusal reply is a shape the sender already reads.
2. IN THE NODE the hold keeps the count and nothing else: the item is not pushed to arrived, the log row says outcome 'held' with no payload (his rule: words go into the traffic log only when they will reasonably be seen), and the counter of consideration (the hourglass) still moves as today.
3. The comment of 1419 becomes true; the design's open line is closed with his ruling (told, not silent) and says so.
4. Nothing else changes: known, admit and drop as today; acquire untouched (S12, the blocked sender under acquire, is its own batch).

WHAT: a relay's owner is set when the relay is installed and in no other way; the relay's first-claim path and its owner-invite checks, a fallback for a token nothing mints any more, are deleted with a test that they are gone, and the relay install gets the one step that writes the owner file from the key it is given, as the face install does. CHECKED by claude-windows at b355e36d:
- The owner is relay-state/owner.json, read by relayAuth (readOwner) and written by writeOwner; it survives bash/update (RELAY-HOST.md). becomeOwner (relay.js 1441) is its only writer in code, and it runs only from the first-claim branch.
- relay.js claimAttempt 1585-1604: a relay with no owner takes a signed claim that redeems an owner invite (invites.isOwnerInvite) and becomes owned; 1658-1660 a leftover owner invite is refused for a member claim; 1759 the owner invite burned. invites.js 97 says the owner invite is "minted by install.js over SSH"; no install.js exists in the tree, so nothing mints one and the branch cannot be taken on a real box. - bash/face-install takes the owner's public key as its first argument and writes owner.json for the face. The relay's install (install-units, start) has no such step: an operator writes owner.json by hand.

DELETE: the firstOwner branch of claimAttempt, becomeOwner, invites.isOwnerInvite and the owner kind of invite, the leftover-owner-invite refusal, the comments naming install.js; the register's 'owner invite required' texts. items.box:
WHAT: the list of relays a node uses (where it claims, acquires, shows presence and searches peers) becomes the node's own state, relay-state/relays.json, read and written through node verbs, and leaves the Natter app's folder. Natter becomes a face over those verbs (A1 of the review, rule 3: no app logic in node or relay).

DECIDED (Andy, 2026-10-10 and 2026-10-11):
- This item at his word.
- Two node verbs, approved by name: relay.search (it exists; it now reads the node's list) and relay.remove (new). No relay.add: a successful claim adds its relay.
- Ownership is written at install and never travels (goal/G16.8); a claim only ever adds a member's relay to the list.
- THE SEED IS TWO RELAYS (2026-10-11): "i say two." A fresh node is seeded with spirit.andyflinn.com and noderoutes.net: "i own the domain name. and i'll use spirit for development and noderoutes.net for the actual site." and "noderoutes.net will not update as often as spirit". noderoutes.net answers nothing yet; "it will exist before end of next week".

- The node seeds relay-state/relays.json with the first relay on a fresh root and reads only that file; shell/natter/relays.json leaves the tree.

- The two error texts lose the path, in the register both sides load.

FOLDED IN: the per-peer counters leave the Contacts folder for node state (A4); the operator pages name the node-state file.

items.title: The node's own packets, marked so no app can forge them (N4)
items.box:
WHAT: the packets the node itself composes and addresses to the owner's shell, published (every server's changed published object on a puppet) and api (the api door's answers), carry an app name today, and a puppet app can post a packet with the same name that the owner's shell cannot tell from the node's; they get a mark only the node can set, so the shell and the doors branch on that mark and on no app name (N4 of the review; the other half of goal/G16.4, "remove it." left this half here).

DECIDED: an item of this goal at Andy's word (2026-10-10, "let's do it that way.": one cleanup item last and three design items, each argued one at a time before it is built). From the review of 2026-10-10 (Andreas Thut, at e8f8ffd).

CHECKED by claude-windows at b355e36d:
- puppetStream.js 56 encodes app 'published' for the owner; shell.js routes a packet whose app is published to onPublished for every element (deliverPackets).
- apiDoor.js 148 encodes its answers with app 'api' and takes only packets whose app is 'api' (167).
- The envelope (client/packet.js) carries app, re, hash and the body; nothing in it says "made by the node", and any app on a puppet posts through the same peerPost under the node's key, so the signature cannot tell them apart either.
- The rule's reasoning (NODE-AND-RELAY.md): system packets carry no app; that is what keeps a puppet from forging them.

ARGUED (2026-10-10): Andy, "i would think that published packets, by definition, reach shell apps, and if the shell apps cannot read and filter them, they're useless. appServer to AppServer communications, why would the shell want to know about them?" and "Server apps hold the node's key." Checked: in code a server app holds no key and asks its node to sign (kernel.js 596), but it runs on the same box as the node and can read the node's key file from disk, so it is trusted as the node is and a mark the node sets is no boundary against it. Decided: "drop it." (Andy, 2026-10-10); the item is dropped from the goal, his delete press closes it; the finding stands only for a puppet that one day runs somebody else's app.

SHAPE (as proposed, not pursued): the plainest candidate is a system kind in the envelope, set only by the node's own encoder path and never by an app's post (peerPost refuses an app packet that claims it), with the shell and the doors reading the kind; an app packet named published or api is then an ordinary app packet nobody answers. It changes the wire for those two packets (flag day).

FILES: client/packet.js, puppetStream.js, apiDoor.js, peerPost.js, client/shell.js (core, grant); a new suite.

items.title: Replay windows on the relay's signatures (S5, S8, S9)
items.box:
WHAT: three places where a signed thing can be replayed inside its time window: a sealed owner post to the relay (S5), a member's stream header on another relay (S8), and a node's own post resent unchanged on retry and after a restart past the window (S9); each gets a nonce or a tighter check so a signature serves once (the replay windows of the review).

DECIDED: an item of this goal at Andy's word (2026-10-10, "let's do it that way.": one cleanup item last and three design items, each argued one at a time before it is built). From the review of 2026-10-10 (Andreas Thut, at e8f8ffd).

CHECKED by claude-windows at b355e36d (the review's lines):
- S5: duplicates are refused only while a request is in flight (router.js 294, 389); a signature stays valid about two minutes (relayAuth.js 126); seal.open's at is never checked for self-addressed verbs (relay.js 3081); relay.js 1959 says a post cannot be replayed at all. Whoever sees a sealed owner post (the TLS terminator, a log) re-sends it: a config restart again, another invite minted, debug toggled.
- S8: the stream signature is 'stream', the key and the minute (relayAuth.js 97), naming no relay and carrying no nonce, and a new stream evicts the old one (presence.js 148); relay A replays a member's stream header on relay B within about three minutes and takes over the member's stream there.
- S9: a post is signed once (peerPost.js 908); retries and queue entries restored after a restart resend the same body; the relay accepts minutes -1, 0 and +1 only and 403 bad post signature is treated as permanent; patienceMs up to ten minutes and the persisted queue almost always end in 403.

ARGUED (2026-10-10): on S8, Andy: "isn't the stream itself already verified though the header?" (it is; the signature names no relay) and "then the header needs a signature from the relay (key)." Decided for S8: the relay's public key goes inside what the member signs for the stream header, and the relay accepts a header only when the key named is its own.

DECIDED NOT TO FIX (Andy, 2026-10-11): S5: "the way i see it, spirit-3 is my box. if the person i rent it from invades my space, they can do WAY worse that resending a dumb request. so i wouldn't fix it. same i someone has a key to my appartement, i just have to trust them. NOT worth fixing." S9: "the other issue, NOT worth fixing, we gain nothing over centralized packet distribution systems." So this item builds S8 alone: the relay's public key inside the signed stream header, the relay accepting only a header naming its own key; a post that waits past the signature window stays refused and dropped as today. The title still names S5 and S9; the rename is his.

SHAPE (as first proposed; only the S8 line is built): a nonce or the hash remembered for the window on self-addressed verbs (S5); the relay's own key in the stream message (S8); a post re-signed at send time, never at queue time (S9). All three change the wire (flag day).

FILES: relayAuth.js, relay.js, router.js, presence.js, peerPost.js (core, grant); a new suite.

items.title: App error codes leave the shared register (A3)
items.box:
WHAT: the shared error register, loaded by node and relay alike, defines codes that belong to apps (the desk's taken, box-moved, not-offered, no-such-item; deskClient's unblocked; chatClerver's peer-blocked; fileServer's pool-full, no-such-file, already-exists), and an app cannot define its own because define throws 'already declared'; the app codes leave the register and an app declares its codes itself (A3 of the review, rule 3: no app logic in node or relay).

DECIDED: an item of this goal at Andy's word (2026-10-10, "let's do it that way.": one cleanup item last and three design items, each argued one at a time before it is built). From the review of 2026-10-10 (Andreas Thut, at e8f8ffd).

CHECKED by claude-windows at b355e36d (the review's lines):
- spiritErrors.js 731-800 defines the app codes; the comment near 802 says the register holds nothing of any app's.
- appServer.js 155 maps only the refusals it knows: remove these codes and every desk, fileServer and chatClerver refusal becomes handler-failed.
- define throws 'already declared', so an app cannot take a code over itself.

DECIDED (Andy, 2026-10-11): "yes. get the bloody app error codes out of the core." and "(i knew this was coming, and I'm glad the fix is forced now.)"; and "and make sure their codes start with \"appServerName: error text\" so the origin of the error is clear." So an app's refusal text is always "<server name>: <error text>", the name put there by appServer from the declaration, never typed by the app, so no app can wear another's name.

SHAPE (decided as proposed): an app declares its own codes to appServer (a declaration beside its verbs, status and text per code), appServer maps a refusal by the app's declaration first and the register second; the app codes leave spiritErrors.js with a test that the register holds none; the desk, deskClient, chatClerver and fileServer carry their declarations. Nothing on the wire changes (the same codes travel).

FILES: spiritErrors.js, appServer.js (core, grant); process/js/desk, deskClient, chatClerver, fileServer declarations; a new suite.

items.title: The verifier pulls, checks and reports on every claim
items.box:
WHAT: Andy's verifier (process/js/deskVerify, on his node) starts on every claim, not only on a verify phase, pulls his tree first when the tree is clean, checks the item, and writes its result on the item every time, so he never has to chase whether and how an item was verified.

DECIDED (Andy, 2026-10-11, under goal/G16.5 and G16.6): "the verifier should fucking listen to the desk at all times, even when idling. stupid thing. then desk-status-changes can trigger pulls and checks."; "my Verifier need to poll for verifications, and pull git when a status change occurs in desk."; "The verifier MUST ALWAYS fucking listen to desk and do that work FIRST."; "it is a loopback poll and costs nothing."; "you'll have to make the verifier FUCKING work. or this shit won't get done." The item was added on that last line. On the Done button (2026-10-11, under goal/G16.6): "only the verifier should give me a done button, that's one way of knowing that the 'Done' offered went through the verifier." Red by claude-windows, build by the other agent.

CHECKED by claude-windows at 0335a26f (deskVerify.js):
- It already polls the desk's changes every watchMs (5 s), idle or not (356, the setInterval at the watcher).
- watched() reacts to three words only: verify.again, phase.done verify with pass true, goal.emptied (370-378). A claim-done press on a plain item is invisible to it, and so is a code item's claim.
- It never pulls: its only git calls are rev-parse HEAD and status --porcelain (98-103), so it measures whatever his tree happens to hold; a claim pushed by an agent is checked against stale code and rejected for a missing suite.
- claimCheck reports by verify.pass or verify.reject on the item (334-339): visible on a code item as its status; a direct call (claim.check over his loopback) answers only the caller and writes nothing on the item.

SHAPE (proposed)
1. THE TRIGGER: watched() also queues an item check on a press whose what is claim-done, on any item; the three existing words stay. One word is still one check (the queue rule of goal/G8.12).
2. THE PULL, FIRST: before every check (item or full run) it runs a pull of his tree, fast-forward only, when status --porcelain is empty; when the tree is dirty it does not pull and checks the tree as it stands, and says so. The command is a manifest value (pull, default "git pull --ff-only --quiet") so a suite can hand a harmless probe instead of touching a real checkout.
3. THE DONE BUTTON COMES ONLY FROM THE VERIFIER (his ruling): on every item, plain or code, a claim no longer brings Done by itself; the desk offers Done only after the verifier's verify.pass on that item (desk.js, today a plain item's claim-done brings Done at once). A rejected check brings no Done and says why.
4. THE RESULT, ON THE ITEM, EVERY TIME: after every check it writes one chat line under the item, by deskVerify: passed or rejected, the commit it checked, whether it pulled or found the tree dirty, and the red suites by name when rejected; a code item also gets verify.pass or verify.reject as today. A direct claim.check writes the same line.

TESTS, red first: spirit/test/deskVerifyOnClaim.js, the fake node of deskVerifyWatch.js: a claim-done press on a plain item with a green test file makes the verifier check it unasked and write a passed line on it; a claim-done on an item whose file is red writes a rejected line naming the suite; the pull probe ran before each check (it writes a marker the suite reads), and a dirty tree (a probe that reports dirty) is checked without the pull and the line says dirty; a code item's verify pass still asks verify.pass and now also writes the line; history before start still triggers nothing. deskVerifyWatch, deskVerifyFull, deskVerifyReject stay green.

FILES: process/js/deskVerify/deskVerify.js and deskVerify.json; process/js/desk/desk.js (Done only after verify.pass); spirit/test/deskVerifyOnClaim.js (new).

NEXT, RULED, NOT YET IN AN ITEM (Andy, 2026-10-11): "the verifier should catch both transition from red to green and vice versa, that way it will verify that the reds are really red." and "so when the reds are pushed, it should verify as well." So when a red phase is passed, the verifier runs that red on his tree and refuses the pass unless it is red; at verify it requires those tests to have flipped to green since (the flips are already in verify.db). Fold into this item or its own: his word.
